mcq.q: What biological example does Licklider (1960) open with to explain symbiosis?
o: The fig tree is pollinated only by the insect Blastophaga grossorum
A bee that takes nectar from many kinds of flowers without depending on any one kind
A small fish that lives in a coral reef and is sheltered by the coral from larger fish
A bird that nests in a tall tree and eats insects living on the tree to feed its young
mcq.e: The paper: "The fig tree is pollinated only by the insect Blastophaga grossorum. The larva of the insect lives in the ovary of the fig tree, and there it gets its food."

mcq.q: According to the paper, what is symbiosis?
o: Competition between two organisms of the same species for food in the same environment
The complete replacement of one organism by a stronger one after a long period of time
The independent existence of two organisms with no interaction between them of any kind
The "living together in intimate association, or even close union, of two dissimilar organisms"
mcq.e: The paper: 'This cooperative "living together in intimate association, or even close union, of two dissimilar organisms" is called symbiosis.'

mcq.q: Which class does man-computer symbiosis belong to, per Licklider?
o: Another name for strong artificial intelligence that fully replaces humans
A subclass of man-machine systems
A form of fully automated computer system that needs no human operator
A wholly new kind of system unrelated to man-machine systems
mcq.e: The paper: '"Man-computer symbiosis" is a subclass of man-machine systems.'

mcq.q: What did Licklider say about the actual state of man-computer symbiosis in 1960?
o: Symbiosis was complete and only needed to be rolled out to government agencies
Many well-working symbiotic systems already existed in large laboratories around the world
At present there are no man-computer symbioses; the paper aims to present the concept
Symbiosis was impossible, and the paper aimed only to criticize the idea
mcq.e: The paper: "At present, however, there are no man-computer symbioses. The purposes of this paper are to present the concept and, hopefully, to foster the development of man-computer symbiosis".

mcq.q: What long-term hope does Licklider state about the partnership?
o: The human brain will be implanted into computers to become part of the machine's memory
Computers will fully replace the human brain in every intellectual task within a few years
Human brains and computers will be coupled tightly
Computers will be used only to store data and will take no part in thinking
mcq.e: The paper: "human brains and computing machines will be coupled together very tightly, and that the resulting partnership will think as no human brain has ever thought".

mcq.q: How does "mechanically extended man" (North) differ from symbiosis?
o: In the older systems human and machine were two different organisms in an equal partnership
In the older systems the computer could think and decide independently without any human
In the older systems the machine supplied all initiative and direction and the human only watched
In the older systems the human supplied initiative, direction, integration and criterion
mcq.e: The paper: "In the man-machine systems of the past, the human operator supplied the initiative, the direction, the integration, and the criterion. The mechanical parts of the systems were mere extensions, first, of the human arm, then of the human eye."

mcq.q: Why is a "mechanically extended man" system not symbiotic?
o: Because that system worked only in large factories and not in offices
Because that system let the operator make no decisions at all in the system
There was only one kind of organism (man), with the rest there only to help
Because that system used machinery too old to link with any modern system
mcq.e: The paper: "There was only one kind of organism—man—and the rest was there only to help him."

mcq.q: What does Licklider say about large computer systems where humans do only what could not be automated?
o: They are perfect symbiotic systems because human and machine share the work sensibly
They are complete AI systems because the machine already does nearly all the work
They are "humanly extended machines" (semi-automatic), not symbiotic systems
They are classic mechanical systems because the operator still uses crude tools
mcq.e: The paper: 'Such systems ("humanly extended machines," North might call them) are not symbiotic systems. They are "semi-automatic" systems, systems that started out to be fully automatic but fell short of the goal.'

mcq.q: Does Licklider claim symbiosis is the ultimate paradigm for complex technological systems?
o: Yes; he asserts machines will never surpass the human brain in any function
No; he thinks that in the long run machines may outdo the brain in most functions
No; he thinks machines will replace humans completely within a few years
Yes; he considers it the permanent optimum and every other system inferior
mcq.e: The paper: "Man-computer symbiosis is probably not the ultimate paradigm for complex technological systems... in due course, electronic or chemical 'machines' will outdo the human brain in most of the functions we now consider exclusively within its province."

mcq.q: What does Gelernter's program illustrate in the paper?
o: A translation program that translated scientific texts with complete accuracy
An IBM-704 geometry theorem-proving program proceeding at about the pace of Brooklyn high school students, making similar errors
A chess program that beat the world champion in an official match
A geometry theorem-proving program that far surpassed the best mathematicians in the world
mcq.e: The paper: "Gelernter's IBM-704 program for proving theorems in plane geometry proceeds at about the same pace as Brooklyn high school students, and makes similar errors."

mcq.q: When did the multidisciplinary group estimate machines alone could do significant thinking?
o: About 1965, leaving about 2 years to develop symbiosis and 3 years to use it
About 1990, leaving about 10 years to develop symbiosis and 5 years to use it
About 2000, leaving about 20 years to develop symbiosis and 30 years to use it
About 1980, leaving about 5 years to develop symbiosis and 15 years to use it
mcq.e: The paper: "it would be 1980 before developments in artificial intelligence make it possible for machines alone to do much thinking or problem solving of military significance. That would leave, say, five years to develop man-computer symbiosis and 15 years to use it."

mcq.q: What does Licklider say about the "15 years" of using symbiosis?
o: The 15 is meaningless and the author says nothing about estimating time
The 15 is certainly too large and in fact only 2 years remain to use symbiosis
The 15 is exactly accurate and has been verified by many independent studies
The 15 may be 10 or 500, but those years should be the most creative
mcq.e: The paper: "The 15 may be 10 or 500, but those years should be intellectually the most creative and exciting in the history of mankind."

mcq.q: What were present-day computers (in Licklider's time) designed mainly to do?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: Simulate human thought and fully replace scientists
Formulate new problems and solve them without any human taking part
Cooperate with humans in forming research questions and scientific hypotheses
Solve preformulated problems or process data by predetermined procedures
mcq.e: The paper: "Present-day computers are designed primarily to solve preformulated problems or to process data according to predetermined procedures."

mcq.q: What is the first main aim of man-computer symbiosis?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: To bring the computer in to store every library book so paper is no longer needed
To bring the computer into the "formulative" parts of technical problems
To bring the computer in to grade and evaluate students' work at school
To bring the computer in to replace scientists in all research work
mcq.e: The paper: "One of the main aims of man-computer symbiosis is to bring the computing machine effectively into the formulative parts of technical problems."

mcq.q: Why are some problems solvable only with machine help in formulating them?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: Because humans lack the memory to remember every scientific and technical problem
Because computers always formulate problems more accurately than humans in every field
Some problems cannot be formulated without machine aid
Because scientific problems are all so simple that computers can solve them at once
mcq.e: The paper: "many problems that can be thought through in advance are very difficult to think through in advance. They would be easier to solve... through an intuitively guided trial-and-error procedure in which the computer cooperated... Other problems simply cannot be formulated without computing-machine aid."

mcq.q: Which quotation from Poincaré is cited?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: "The question is not, 'What is the answer?' The question is, 'What is the question?'"
"A good question is better than an answer, and answers can always be found in books"
"Every scientific problem has exactly one answer that a computer can find"
"Computers will never replace the intuition of the mathematician in research"
mcq.e: The paper: 'Poincaré... said, "The question is not, \'What is the answer?\' The question is, \'What is the question?\'"'

mcq.q: What is the second main aim of symbiosis?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: To bring computers into designing other computers faster and cheaper than today's
To bring computers into storing military data so it is better protected from the enemy
To bring computers into thinking that must occur in "real time"
To bring computers into teaching primary school children in place of teachers
mcq.e: The paper: "bring computing machines effectively into processes of thinking that must go on in 'real time,' time that moves too fast to permit using computers in conventional ways."

mcq.q: What does the example of directing a battle with a computer on a conventional schedule illustrate?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: Computers always calculate faster than any general so the battle is always won
Current use is far too slow (formulate today, programmer tomorrow, result next week)
Programmers always produce better tactics than computers in every combat situation
The battle cannot be simulated on a computer because it is too complex for the machine
mcq.e: The paper: "You formulate your problem today. Tomorrow you spend with a programmer. Next week the computer devotes 5 minutes to assembling your program and 47 seconds to calculating the answer... Obviously, the battle would be over before the second step in its planning was begun."

mcq.q: Licklider wants thinking with a computer to be like thinking with whom?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: A rival who competes with you to find the solution faster than you
A subordinate who only follows orders and offers no opinions
A colleague whose competence supplements your own
A teacher far more capable than you who teaches you step by step
mcq.e: The paper: "To think in interaction with a computer in the same way that you think with a colleague whose competence supplements your own will require much tighter coupling between man and machine".

mcq.q: How did Licklider gather his "time-and-motion" evidence on technical thinking?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: By interviewing thousands of engineers about how they spend their working day
By observing hundreds of scientists in large laboratories over many years
By tracking himself (one person) during the hours he regarded as work, in spring
By using brain-activity devices to record the thinking of many participants
mcq.e: The paper: "In the spring and summer of 1957, therefore, I tried to keep track of what one moderately technical person actually did during the hours he regarded as devoted to work... I served as my own subject."

mcq.q: What does Licklider admit about his self-measurement?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: He believed the one-person sample fully represented every researcher in every field
He admitted no limits and treated the result as absolutely certain
He rechecked results with a large sample of hundreds of people and found them identical
He knew the sampling was inadequate (one person, himself)
mcq.e: The paper: "Although I was aware of the inadequacy of the sampling, I served as my own subject... Perhaps my spectrum is not typical—I hope it is not, but I fear it is."

mcq.q: About what percentage of Licklider's "thinking" time went to getting into position to think, decide or learn?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: About 85%
About 15%
About 50%
About 5%
mcq.e: The paper: "About 85 per cent of my 'thinking' time was spent getting into a position to think, to make a decision, to learn something I needed to know."

mcq.q: If 85% went to preparation, how much remained for the main activity?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: About 5%
About 15%
About 50%
About 85%
mcq.e: 100 minus 85 is 15 percent; this is a one-person self-measurement.

mcq.q: Which example in the paper shows data preparation taking longer than analysis?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: Comparing six determinations of a speech-intelligibility function: hours of calculating to make them comparable, then seconds to see what he needed
Writing a long scientific paper for days, then only seconds to mail it
Assembling a large computer for months, then only seconds to switch it on and use it
Translating a book from a foreign language for years, then seconds to read it
mcq.e: The paper: "it was necessary to compare six experimental determinations of a function relating speech-intelligibility to speech-to-noise ratio... Several hours of calculating were required to get the data into comparable form. When they were in comparable form, it took only a few seconds to determine what I needed to know."

mcq.q: What did Licklider conclude about his "thinking" time?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: It was devoted mainly to teaching and guiding students and young colleagues
It was devoted mainly to clerical or mechanical activities such as searching, calculating, plotting
It was devoted mainly to creating new ideas and producing breakthrough scientific theories
It was devoted mainly to meetings and exchanging views with colleagues in his group
mcq.e: The paper: '"thinking" time was devoted mainly to activities that were essentially clerical or mechanical: searching, calculating, plotting, transforming, determining the logical or dynamic consequences of a set of assumptions or hypotheses'.

mcq.q: What did Licklider remark about his choices of what to attempt?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: They were determined by the time available in the day, unrelated to clerical feasibility
They were determined wholly by intellectual capability, unaffected by clerical factors
They were determined by superiors and colleagues rather than by his own choice
They were determined "to an embarrassingly great extent" by clerical feasibility rather than intellectual capability
mcq.e: The paper: "my choices of what to attempt and what not to attempt were determined to an embarrassingly great extent by considerations of clerical feasibility, not intellectual capability."

mcq.q: What is the main suggestion drawn from the self-measurement?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: two aims and the evidence
o: The operations filling most "thinking" time are ones machines can perform more effectively than people
Scientists' thinking time is so small it can be ignored when designing man-computer systems
The operations filling most "thinking" time are ones only people can do
People should spend more time searching for information instead of asking a computer
mcq.e: The paper: "the operations that fill most of the time allegedly devoted to technical thinking are operations that can be performed more effectively by machines than by men."

mcq.q: How does Licklider describe the human nervous system compared with computers?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: As noisy narrow-band devices with very many parallel
As slow devices with perfect accuracy in all mathematical calculations
As wide-band highly accurate devices with a single active channel
As devices like computers but with far larger memory
mcq.e: The paper: "men are noisy narrow-band devices, but their nervous systems have very many parallel and simultaneously active channels."

mcq.q: What is a characteristic of computers compared with people, per Licklider?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: Very creative, producing scientific ideas humans have not thought of
Very fast and accurate, but constrained to perform only one or a few elementary operations at a time
Very flexible, reprogramming themselves on new information without guidance
Very slow but able to do thousands of different calculations at once with high accuracy
mcq.e: The paper: "Relative to men, computing machines are very fast and very accurate, but they are constrained to perform only one or a few elementary operations at a time."

mcq.q: Who can "program themselves contingently"?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: Neither, since every activity is fully predetermined
People: flexible, adjusting on the basis of newly received information
Computers: adjusting their programs on information newly received from the user
Both people and computers to the same degree in every situation
mcq.e: The paper: 'Men are flexible, capable of "programming themselves contingently" on the basis of newly received information. Computing machines are single-minded, constrained by their "preprogramming."'

mcq.q: How do human and computer languages differ per Licklider?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: People and computers use the same kind of language, so communication is no problem
People speak redundant languages with 20 to 60 elementary symbols; computers "speak" nonredundant languages
People speak nonredundant languages of two symbols; computers speak redundant languages of hundreds of symbols
People use mathematical language while computers use natural language with the full human vocabulary
mcq.e: The paper: "Men naturally speak redundant languages organized around unitary objects and coherent actions and employing 20 to 60 elementary symbols. Computers 'naturally' speak nonredundant languages, usually with only two elementary symbols".

mcq.q: What do the differences between people and machines suggest about cooperation?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: Potential supplementation: machines do readily many things hard for people
People always outperform machines at every job, so no cooperation is needed
Machines always outperform people at every job, so only machines should be used
People and machines are alike, so they can replace one another entirely in every job
mcq.e: The paper: "Computing machines can do readily, well, and rapidly many things that are difficult or impossible for man, and men can do readily and well, though not rapidly, many things that are difficult or impossible for computers. That suggests that a symbiotic cooperation... would be of great value."

mcq.q: In the anticipated division of labor, who sets the goals and supplies motivation?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: People, at least in the early years
Both equally and identically
Computers, from the early years of the partnership
Neither, since goals are fixed in the program
mcq.e: The paper: "Men will set the goals and supply the motivations, of course, at least in the early years."

mcq.q: What will people do in the partnership per Licklider?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: Only perform fast arithmetic that computers of that time could not yet do
Only record results and enter data while the computer does all the reasoning
Formulate hypotheses, ask questions, think of mechanisms and models, define criteria
Only maintain and repair the computers when they break down
mcq.e: The paper: "They will formulate hypotheses. They will ask questions. They will think of mechanisms, procedures, and models... they will define criteria and serve as evaluators, judging the contributions of the equipment and guiding the general line of thought."

mcq.q: What special situations will people handle?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: Very-low-probability situations when they actually arise
Only situations needing high-precision calculation that people do better than computers
No situations, since computers will handle everything that can happen
Only very common situations for which the computer already has a routine
mcq.e: The paper: "men will handle the very-low-probability situations when such situations do actually arise... Men will fill in the gaps, either in the problem solution or in the computer program, when the computer has no mode or routine that is applicable".

mcq.q: What will computers do?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: Only control input and output equipment and process no scientific data
Set the goals, decide the criteria and give the final evaluation of every result
Only store books and documents without taking part in any reasoning
Convert hypotheses into testable models, simulate, transform data, plot graphs
mcq.e: The paper: "The information-processing equipment... will convert hypotheses into testable models and then test the models against data... It will simulate the mechanisms and models... transform data, plot graphs... it will carry out the routinizable, clerical operations that fill the intervals between decisions."

mcq.q: What status will the machine accept in diagnosis, pattern matching and relevance recognition?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: It will have a fully equal status with people in all diagnosis and recognition
It will not be allowed to take part because its accuracy is still too low
It will do as much as profitably possible
It will hold the leading status, with people just following its diagnoses
mcq.e: The paper: "it will do as much diagnosis, pattern matching, and relevance recognizing as it profitably can, but it will accept a clearly secondary status in those areas."

mcq.q: Why will the contributions of people and machines be hard to separate in many operations?
mcq.sec: Licklider 1960: capabilities and division of labor
o: Because both may come up with relevant precedents or the computer may suggest a course of action matching the person's intuition
Because computers are always slower than people and must wait until people finish
Because people do not care about the machine's contribution to solving the problem
Because people and machines always work in different rooms so cannot be compared
mcq.e: The paper: "the contributions of human operators and equipment will blend together so completely in many operations that it will be difficult to separate them neatly in analysis."

mcq.q: How does Licklider propose to handle the "speed mismatch"?
o: Making computers slower to match the speed of humans working with them
Teaching people to calculate faster to keep up with computers
Giving each person a private computer with no sharing among people
Time-sharing: the computer divides its time among many users to balance speed
mcq.e: The paper: "Any present-day large-scale computer is too fast and too costly for real-time cooperative thinking with one man. Clearly... the computer must divide its time among many users. Time-sharing systems are currently under active development."

mcq.q: What is the "thinking center" Licklider envisions?
o: A center combining library functions, information storage and retrieval
A single large computer in the capital used only by top government agencies
A new university that trains programmers for large technology companies
A building used only for conferences and scientific workshops among researchers
mcq.e: The paper: 'a "thinking center" that will incorporate the functions of present-day libraries together with anticipated advances in information storage and retrieval and the symbiotic functions... a network of such centers, connected to one another by wide-band communication lines'.

mcq.q: What does the paper say about storing technical literature in computer memory?
o: None would be stored, as memory was far too small and expensive for this
All technical and scientific literature would be stored and printed books abandoned
Only authors' names would be stored, without content or citations
Not all of it would be stored, only the succinct parts such as quantitative material
mcq.e: The paper: "we shall not store all the technical and scientific papers in computer memory. We may store the parts that can be summarized most succinctly—the quantitative parts and the reference citations—but not the whole. Books... will continue to be functionally important".

mcq.q: How was the cost of storing an appreciable fraction of technical literature estimated?
o: Millions of bits and a few thousand dollars, needing only a medium computer
Thousands of bits and a few hundred dollars, within reach of any laboratory
Impossible to estimate because nobody had studied the problem
Billions of bits and billions of dollars unless things change markedly
mcq.e: The paper: "When we start to think of storing any appreciable fraction of a technical literature in computer memory, we run into billions of bits and, unless things change markedly, billions of dollars."

mcq.q: Which two important kinds of memory does Licklider name?
o: The person's memory and the machine's memory shared during cooperation
"Indelible" memory (write once, read indefinitely)
Fast cache memory and slow disk memory used interchangeably by computers
Short-term and long-term memory of the humans working with computers
mcq.e: The paper: "a very important section of memory will be permanent: part indelible memory and part published memory. The computer will be able to write once into indelible memory, and then read back indefinitely... Published memory will be 'read-only' memory."

mcq.q: What does memory organization for symbiosis require?
o: Information sorted by time of entry and never changed
Information retrieved by serial number only, not by name or pattern
Information retrieved serially from start to end because it is simplest and cheapest
Information retrievable by name and by pattern, much faster than serial search
mcq.e: The paper: "Implicit in the idea of man-computer symbiosis are the requirements that information be retrievable both by name and by pattern and that it be accessible through procedure much faster than serial search."

mcq.q: How is Fredkin's "trie memory" described?
o: It stores data in a two-dimensional table of rows and columns like a spreadsheet
It stores only functions and no arguments, using fixed addresses for each function
It stores data in order of entry like a diary of the computer
It stores both arguments and functions in a branching, tree-like structure
mcq.e: The paper: "The trie memory system, on the other hand, stores both the functions and the arguments. The argument is introduced into the memory one character at a time, starting at a standard initial register... the branching storage structure... resembles a tree."

mcq.q: What is an advantage of trie memory named in the paper?
o: Arguments sharing initial characters share the storage for them
It requires reserving space for every possible argument before any is stored
It allows only fixed-length arguments that must be specified in advance
It is most efficient for small memories and less efficient as memory grows
mcq.e: The paper: "If two arguments have initial characters in common, they use the same storage space for those characters. The lengths of the arguments need not be the same, and need not be specified in advance... No room in storage is reserved for or used by any argument until it is actually stored."

mcq.q: What does Licklider consider possibly the most serious obstacle to true symbiosis?
o: A shortage of people capable of programming the big computers in laboratories
Public opposition to using computers in intellectual work
The high cost of electronic components used to build computers at the time
The basic dissimilarity between human and computer languages
mcq.e: The paper: "The basic dissimilarity between human languages and computer languages may be the most serious obstacle to true symbiosis."

mcq.q: How do instructions to computers differ from instructions to humans?
o: Instructions to computers specify courses (steps and order); instructions to humans specify goals
Both specify exact steps and sequence precisely
Instructions to computers specify goals; instructions to humans specify courses and steps
Both specify only general goals with nothing on how to do them
mcq.e: The paper: "instructions directed to computers specify courses; instructions directed to human beings specify goals."

mcq.q: What does the Boston to Los Angeles example illustrate?
o: People think more naturally in terms of goals than in terms of precisely specified routes
People always need a detailed step-by-step route before beginning any trip
Computers always find the shortest route and people need only follow without thinking
Going from Boston to Los Angeles is an optimization problem only computers can solve
mcq.e: The paper: "Men appear to think more naturally and easily in terms of goals than in terms of courses... Who, for example, would depart from Boston for Los Angeles with a detailed specification of the route?"

mcq.q: What are the two paths toward instructing computers by goals?
o: Self-copying programs; and programs that delete unneeded parts of themselves
Automatic translation programs; and syntax-checking programs for programming languages
Problem-solving, hill-climbing, self-organizing programs
Memory-management programs; and programs managing the computer's input and output devices
mcq.e: The paper: "The first involves problem-solving, hill-climbing, self-organizing programs. The second involves real-time concatenation of preprogrammed segments and closed subroutines which the human operator can designate and call into action simply by name."

mcq.q: How does Licklider judge input and output equipment of the time?
o: An area people do not care about since punched cards suffice
The most advanced area, with many graphics and voice devices common on every machine
The least advanced area; almost only an electric typewriter for immediate man-machine communication
A finished area needing no improvement for symbiosis
mcq.e: The paper: "The department of data processing that seems least advanced... is the one that deals with input and output equipment... there is almost no provision for any more effective, immediate man-machine communication than can be achieved with an electric typewriter."

mcq.q: What is the purpose of the proposed "desk-surface display and control"?
o: For man and computer to draw graphs and pictures and write notes
To print documents faster than ordinary printers in offices of the time
To store technical drawings safely and conveniently in the computer's memory
To let users sit comfortably while using a computer for many hours
mcq.e: The paper: "for effective man-computer interaction, it will be necessary for the man and the computer to draw graphs and pictures and to write notes and equations to each other on the same display surface."

mcq.q: How does Engelbart (1962) define "augmenting human intellect"?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Increasing a person's capability to approach a complex problem situation
Raising native human intelligence by changing the biological structure of the brain
Teaching people isolated clever tricks that help them remember faster in specific cases
Replacing people with computers in all intellectual work to reach results fastest
mcq.e: The paper: '"By augmenting human intellect we mean increasing the capability of a man to approach a complex problem situation, to gain comprehension to suit his particular needs, and to derive solutions to problems."'

mcq.q: What is the increased capability understood to be a mixture of?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Only faster memorization with no other change in comprehension or problem solving
More rapid and better comprehension, useful comprehension of formerly too-complex situations, speedier and better solutions, and solutions to seemingly insoluble problems
Only faster reading with no other change in comprehension or problem solving
Only faster calculation with no other change in comprehension or problem solving
mcq.e: The paper: "more rapid comprehension, better comprehension, the possibility of gaining a useful degree of comprehension in a situation that previously was too complex, speedier solutions, better solutions, and the possibility of finding solutions to problems that before seemed insoluble."

mcq.q: Which "complex situations" does Engelbart include?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Only simple administrative procedures that civil servants perform in government offices
Only textbook math problems that students do in class every day
Professional problems of diplomats, executives, scientists, attorneys and designers
Only intellectual games such as chess and go played for leisure at weekends
mcq.e: The paper: "complex situations we include the professional problems of diplomats, executives, social scientists, life scientists, physical scientists, attorneys, designers—whether the problem situation exists for twenty minutes or twenty years."

mcq.q: What does Engelbart make clear about the scope of his goal?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Merely a few small tricks useful in some specific everyday work situations
Merely buying the latest electronic equipment for offices and laboratories
Merely changing an agency's administrative procedures without involving people
Not isolated clever tricks but "a way of life" in an integrated domain where hunches coexist with powerful tools
mcq.e: The paper: "We do not speak of isolated clever tricks that help in particular situations. We refer to a way of life in an integrated domain where hunches, cut-and-try, intangibles, and the human feel for a situation usefully coexist with powerful concepts, streamlined terminology and notation, sophisticated methods, and high-powered electronic aids."

mcq.q: What are the four classes of augmentation means (LAMT)?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Artifacts, Language, Methodology and Training
Analysis, Logic, Mathematics and Technology
Assistance, Learning, Motivation and Testing
Attention, Language, Memory and Thinking
mcq.e: The paper defines four classes: "Artifacts... Language... Methodology... Training".

mcq.q: What are "Artifacts" for Engelbart?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: The methods, procedures and strategies used to organize problem-solving activity
The conditioning needed to bring skill in using the means to practical effectiveness
Physical objects designed for comfort, for manipulating things or materials
The way an individual divides the world into concepts and symbols used for thinking
mcq.e: The paper: "Artifacts—physical objects designed to provide for human comfort, for the manipulation of things or materials, and for the manipulation of symbols."

mcq.q: What is "Language" for Engelbart?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: How the individual parcels the world into concepts used to model it
The methods and strategies an individual uses to organize problem-solving work
Physical objects designed to manipulate things, materials and symbols for people
The training needed for a person to be effective in using the augmentation means
mcq.e: The paper: "Language—the way in which the individual parcels out the picture of his world into the concepts that his mind uses to model that world, and the symbols that he attaches to those concepts and uses in consciously manipulating the concepts ('thinking')."

mcq.q: What is "Methodology" for Engelbart?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: The methods, procedures and strategies with
The conditioning needed to bring skill in using tools to practical effectiveness
Physical objects designed for comfort and manipulating things, materials and symbols
The way the individual divides the world into concepts and symbols used in thinking
mcq.e: The paper: "Methodology—the methods, procedures, strategies, etc., with which an individual organizes his goal-centered (problem-solving) activity."

mcq.q: What is "Training" for Engelbart?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Memorizing rules and definitions from textbooks and instruction manuals
Trial and error with new tools without guidance from anyone
The conditioning needed to bring skill in using language, artifacts
Testing and grading a user's ability after using the tools
mcq.e: The paper: "Training—the conditioning needed by the human being to bring his skills in using Means 1, 2, and 3 to the point where they are operationally effective."

mcq.q: What system does Engelbart envision improving?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: The H-LAM/T system: a trained human together with his language, artifacts
Only the software, not counting hardware, people or working methods
Only the computer, not counting the human, language or working methods
Only the human, not counting the tools or language used to work
mcq.e: The paper: "The system we want to improve can thus be visualized as a trained human being together with his artifacts, language, and methodology" (HLAMT: Human using Language, Artifacts, Methodology, in which he is Trained).

mcq.q: Which entity has the "amplified intelligence" per Engelbart?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Only the computer, after installation of smarter software
Only the human, after being trained to use new tools
Only the language, after adding many new symbols and terms
The whole H-LAM/T system, not the human alone
mcq.e: The paper: "What possesses the amplified intelligence is the resulting HLAMT system in which the LAMT augmentation means represent the amplifier of the human's intelligence."

mcq.q: What does Engelbart envision as the artifacts of the new system?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Only telephones and fax machines for quick contact among work groups
Computers and computer-controlled information storage, handling
Only digitized books and libraries reachable remotely by everyone
Only improved pens and paper of higher quality and lower cost
mcq.e: The paper: "The explicit new system we contemplate will involve as artifacts computers and computer-controlled information-storage, information-handling, and information-display devices."

mcq.q: How is the structure of an individual's capabilities described?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: A flat list of independent skills with no relation among them
An interknit hierarchical structure (a repertoire like a tool kit) resting on basic capabilities in the person or in artifacts
A structure of only memory and attention with no higher-order capabilities
A fixed innate structure that learning or new tools cannot change
mcq.e: The paper: "each individual develops a certain repertoire of process capabilities... like a tool kit... the entire repertoire represents an interknit, hierarchical structure".

mcq.q: What does writing prose illustrate about capability structure?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: It is independent of all other processes and cannot combine with any of them
It is a process only professional writers have and ordinary people lack
It is the simplest process people can do and needs no subprocess
It is a high-order process using many subprocesses
mcq.e: The paper: "When a man writes prose text, a reasonably high-order process, he makes use of many processes as subprocesses that are common to other high-order processes... The process of writing is utilized as a subprocess within many different processes of still higher order".

mcq.q: Why does changing one level (language, artifacts or methodology) call for a systems approach?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: The levels are wholly independent so each can change without affecting the others
A change at one level always seriously lowers the effectiveness of the entire system
Only the artifacts level can change; language and methodology are fixed
A change at one level affects the others in the capability hierarchy
mcq.e: The paper: "any potential change in language, artifact, or methodology... brings out the strong interrelationship of these three augmentation means" (in the capability hierarchy).

mcq.q: How did Engelbart first react to the phrase "intelligence amplifier" (Ross Ashby)?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: He did not know the phrase and had never heard of Ross Ashby in this field
He rejected it completely and never used it in the whole report
He accepted it at once because it describes raising native intelligence exactly
He rejected it because the aim was a better match between existing intelligence
mcq.e: The paper: "at first this term was rejected on the grounds that in our view one's only hope was to make a better match between existing human intelligence and the problems... But deriving the concepts... has shown us that indeed this term does seem applicable to our objective."

mcq.q: Does "intelligence amplification" mean raising native intelligence?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: No; it only makes people work faster without changing intellectual capability
No; it means organizing intellectual capabilities into higher levels of synergistic structuring so the system shows more intelligence than an unaided human
Yes; it replaces human intelligence with machine intelligence entirely
Yes; it directly raises native intelligence by changing brain chemistry
mcq.e: The paper: "Accepting the term 'intelligence amplification' does not imply any attempt to increase native human intelligence... we will have amplified the intelligence of the human by organizing his intellectual capabilities into higher levels of synergistic structuring."

mcq.q: Where does the principle of "synergistic structuring" come from?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: From traditional teaching methods in schools around the world
From modern business management principles in large corporations
From the way natural evolution built the basic human capabilities
From optimization algorithms in applied mathematics and computer science
mcq.e: The paper: "In amplifying our intelligence we are applying the principle of synergistic structuring that was followed by natural evolution in developing the basic human capabilities."

mcq.q: What does Engelbart use the Whorfian hypothesis to point out?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: The manner of external symbol manipulation affects neither language nor thought
Language does not affect how people think and serves only for communication
There are two ways external symbol manipulation can affect thinking: directly
Thought completely determines language, which cannot influence thought back
mcq.e: The paper: "The direct effect of the external-symbol-manipulation means upon language would produce an indirect effect upon the way of thinking via the Whorfian-hypothesis linkage. There would then be two ways for the manner in which our external symbol manipulation was done to affect our thinking."

mcq.q: What does the "brick tied to a pencil" experiment illustrate?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: Handwriting is always faster than typewriting for every kind of task
People cannot adapt to any new writing tool other than the traditional pencil
With the same basic capability, changing the tool changes results: writing with the brick-pencil is slower and less precise
The brick-pencil makes writing faster and more precise than an ordinary pencil in all cases
mcq.e: The paper: "We fastened a pencil to a brick and experimented... with the brick-pencil we are slower and less precise. If we want to hurry, ... the brick-pencil tires the untrained hand and arm."

mcq.q: According to Engelbart, is an "argument" serial in nature?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: No; conceptually it is not a serial affair, though we write it serially because paper
Yes; an argument is always a serial chain of steps from premise to conclusion
Yes; an argument can be presented in only one order chosen by the author
No; an argument is only a set of disconnected statements with no relations
mcq.e: The paper: "Conceptually speaking, however, an argument is not a serial affair. It is sequential because some statements have to follow others, but this doesn't imply that its nature is necessarily serial."

mcq.q: What is the architect scenario in the paper used for?
mcq.sec: Engelbart 1962: definition and the H-LAM/T system
o: To convey a feeling for the richness and promise of possibilities through a fictional dialogue
To prove experimentally that architects work ten times faster with computers
To report survey results from architects who had used computers in design
To describe in technical detail how to build a computer for architectural design
mcq.e: The paper: Section III is presented "in fiction-dialogue style as a mechanism for transmitting a feeling for the richness and promise of the possibilities".

mcq.q: Which group does Engelbart recommend augmenting first?
o: Physicians and medical researchers
Teachers and university students
Computer programmers
Diplomats and executives
mcq.e: The paper: "We recommend the particular task of computer programming for this purpose".

mcq.q: What is one reason for choosing programmers?
o: They earn the highest pay so they can buy new tools without funding
They have never used computers so their reactions are objective
They work on many large realistic problems that can be solved without interaction with others, easing experiments
They are the largest group in society so results apply to everyone
mcq.e: The paper: "The programmer works on many problems, including large and realistic ones, which can be solved without interaction with other humans. This eases the experimental problem."

mcq.q: What other reason makes programmers suitable?
o: They have never used computers so they learn new tools without old habits
They are the only group able to fund themselves in Engelbart's research program
They need no training to use the new tools because the tools are easy for everyone
They already work in formal methodologies with computers, so new tools seem less radical
mcq.e: The paper: "know how to work in formal methodologies with computers, and most of them are associated with activities that have to have computers anyway, so that the new techniques, concepts, methods, and equipment will not seem so radical to them and will be relatively easy for them to learn and acquire."

mcq.q: What is the "regenerative feature" of the research program?
o: The program automatically replaces old researchers with new ones
Good results feed back to improve the researchers' own tools
The program automatically generates new budgets from the profit of products sold
The program automatically repeats old experiments to check their results
mcq.e: The paper: "our researchers are developing means to increase the effectiveness of humans dealing with complex intellectual problems, and our researchers are dealing with complex intellectual problems. In other words, they are developing better tools for a class to which they themselves belong."

mcq.q: What strategic precept about the order of gains does Engelbart give?
o: Pursue the hardest gains first since they are the most scientifically significant
Wait until computers are smart and large enough before developing augmentation systems
Wait to finish all basic research on the human brain before making any tools
Pursue the quickest gains first, then use the increased effectiveness to pursue successive gains
mcq.e: The paper: "One of its important precepts is to pursue the quickest gains first and use the increased intellectual effectiveness thus derived to help pursue successive gains."

mcq.q: Which conclusion addresses whether we must wait to understand the brain and for smarter machines?
o: We must wait until AI reaches human level before developing these systems
We need not wait: economically feasible augmentation systems can begin from what we now know and have
We must wait for computers to be much faster and larger to avoid waste
We must wait to understand all mental processes to avoid theoretical mistakes
mcq.e: The paper: "we do not have to wait until we learn how the human mental processes work, we do not have to wait until we learn how to make computers more intelligent or bigger or faster, we can begin developing powerful and economically feasible augmentation systems on the basis of what we now know and have."

mcq.q: Why does Engelbart say any possibility of improving human problem-solving deserves serious consideration?
o: Because augmentation systems cost so little that any organization can build them
Because human problem-solving capability may be the most important resource society possesses
Because computers will soon replace humans, so they must be augmented first
Because social problems are getting simpler and need fewer resources to solve
mcq.e: The paper: "man's problem-solving capability represents possibly the most important resource possessed by society."

mcq.q: What is the opening question of Clark and Chalmers (1998)?
o: "How does language affect the way people think?"
"From what brain processes is human consciousness made?"
"Can computers think the way humans do?"
"Where does the mind stop and the rest of the world begin?"
mcq.e: The paper: "Where does the mind stop and the rest of the world begin?"

mcq.q: What two standard answers does the paper give?
o: The boundary is skin and skull; or externalism about meaning (meaning is not in the head) carried over to mind
The boundary is language; or the boundary is the social rules of a community
The boundary is consciousness; or the boundary is the unconscious mind
The boundary is the brain; or the boundary is the whole central nervous system
mcq.e: The paper: "Some accept the boundaries of skin and skull... Others are impressed by arguments suggesting that the meaning of our words 'just ain't in the head', and hold that this externalism about meaning carries over into an externalism about mind."

mcq.q: What third position do the authors propose?
o: Dualism, holding mind and body are wholly separate entities
Active externalism, based on the environment's active role in driving cognitive processes
Strict internalism, holding all mental states lie wholly in the head
Passive externalism, based on distant historical features of the environment
mcq.e: The paper: "We advocate a very different sort of externalism: an active externalism, based on the active role of the environment in driving cognitive processes."

mcq.q: What is drawn from the three problem-solving (rotation) cases?
o: The three are alike in computational structure
None of the three is cognition because all use outside devices or technology
Only mental rotation is cognition; the other two are not
Only the neural implant case is cognition, since the device is inside the body
mcq.e: The paper: "We suggest that all three cases are similar... If the rotation in case (3) is cognitive, by what right do we count case (2) as fundamentally different? We cannot simply point to the skin/skull boundary as justification, since the legitimacy of that boundary is precisely what is at issue."

mcq.q: According to Kirsh and Maglio (1994), how long does physically rotating a Tetris shape 90 degrees take (plus button selection)?
o: About 1000 milliseconds to rotate plus about 200 milliseconds to select the button
About 300 milliseconds to rotate with no time to select the button
About 100 milliseconds to rotate plus about 200 milliseconds to select the button
About 10 milliseconds to rotate plus about 20 milliseconds to select the button
mcq.e: The paper: "the physical rotation of a shape through 90 degrees takes about 100 milliseconds, plus about 200 milliseconds to select the button."

mcq.q: How long does mental rotation of the same result take?
o: About 10 milliseconds
About 100 milliseconds
About 1000 milliseconds
About 300 milliseconds
mcq.e: The paper: "To achieve the same result by mental rotation takes about 1000 milliseconds."

mcq.q: Roughly how many times faster is physical rotation (300 ms) than mental rotation (1000 ms)?
o: About 10 times
About 1.3 times
About 33 times
About 3.3 times
mcq.e: 1000 divided by 300 is about 3.33.

mcq.q: What is an "epistemic action"?
o: An action that alters the world because the physical change is desirable for its own sake
An action of memorizing important information into one's long-term memory
An action of consciously thinking about what one knows and does not know
An action that alters the world to aid and augment cognitive processes such as recognition
mcq.e: The paper: "Epistemic actions alter the world so as to aid and augment cognitive processes such as recognition and search. Merely pragmatic actions, by contrast, alter the world because some physical change is desirable for its own sake".

mcq.q: Which example is a merely pragmatic action?
o: Putting cement into a hole in a dam
Rotating a shape on screen to see whether it fits a slot
Rearranging letter tiles on the tray to prompt word recall in Scrabble
Using pen and paper to perform long multiplication
mcq.e: The paper: "Merely pragmatic actions... alter the world because some physical change is desirable for its own sake (e.g., putting cement into a hole in a dam)."

mcq.q: How is the parity principle of Clark and Chalmers stated?
o: Only processes occurring in the head are cognitive, with no exceptions
Every part of the external world is part of cognition no matter how it functions
If a part of the world plays a role that, done in the head, we would call cognitive
Every cognitive process must be conscious to count as truly cognitive
mcq.e: The paper: "If, as we confront some task, a part of the world functions as a process which, were it done in the head, we would have no hesitation in recognizing as part of the cognitive process, then that part of the world is (so we claim) part of the cognitive process. Cognitive processes ain't (all) in the head!"

mcq.q: How does active externalism differ from Putnam and Burge's externalism?
o: Active externalism holds meaning is in the head while Putnam and Burge hold it is outside
Active externalism applies only to computers and not to humans
The two are the same and differ only in name
In active externalism external features have immediate causal impact on cognition; in Putnam
mcq.e: The paper: "In the cases we describe, by contrast, the relevant external features are active, playing a crucial role in the here-and-now... In the Putnam/Burge cases... the relevant external features are passive."

mcq.q: What happens if the external component of a coupled system is removed?
o: The system's competence rises because there are fewer factors interfering
The system's behavioral competence drops
The system's competence is unchanged because the brain will compensate
The system stops working completely and cannot recover in any case
mcq.e: The paper: "If we remove the external component the system's behavioural competence will drop, just as it would if we removed part of its brain."

mcq.q: What does the Scrabble example illustrate?
o: Scrabble tiles are only for fun and unrelated to cognitive processes
The rearrangement of tiles on the tray is not part of action; it is part of thought
Scrabble needs only vocabulary memory and no physical action
Good Scrabble players calculate everything in their heads without moving tiles
mcq.e: The paper: "In a very real sense, the re-arrangement of tiles on the tray is not part of action; it is part of thought."

mcq.q: How do the authors answer the objection that cognition is tied to consciousness?
o: Consciousness can extend outside the head, so extended cognition has extended consciousness
Not every cognitive process is conscious; many, such as memory retrieval and skill acquisition
Cognition always needs consciousness, so processes outside the head cannot be cognitive
The objection cannot be answered and the authors concede their argument is refuted
mcq.e: The paper: "not every cognitive process, at least on standard usage, is a conscious process. It is widely accepted that all sorts of processes beyond the borders of consciousness play a crucial role in cognitive processing: in the retrieval of memories, linguistic processes, and skill acquisition."

mcq.q: What does the "Naked Mind" (portability) objection claim?
o: Real cognition exists only with outside tools and vanishes when there are none
Real cognition occurs only during sleep when the brain is unaffected by outside factors
Real cognition is the basic package of resources we always carry
Real cognition is a social process between many people and absent in individuals
mcq.e: The paper: "what keeps real cognitive processes in the head is the requirement that cognitive processes be portable... a package of resources and operations we can always bring to bear on a cognitive task, regardless of the local environment. On this view, the trouble with coupled systems is that they are too easily decoupled."

mcq.q: What is the authors' answer to the portability objection?
o: Portability means nothing and the authors ignore this objection completely
Portability is the only criterion and no outside tool ever meets it
What matters is reliable coupling, which can also be with the environment
The biological brain is perfectly portable so it cannot be compared with outside tools
mcq.e: The paper: "for coupled systems to be relevant to the core of cognition, reliable coupling is required. It happens that most reliable coupling takes place within the brain, but there can easily be reliable coupling with the environment as well."

mcq.q: Why does occasional decoupling not undermine the authors' claim?
o: The biological brain never loses capacities, so it cannot be compared with outside tools
The biological brain also loses capacities temporarily in sleep, intoxication and emotion
Outside tools are never lost or broken in any circumstance
Decoupling happens only to people with Alzheimer's and not to anyone else
mcq.e: The paper: "the biological brain is in similar danger, and occasionally loses capacities temporarily in episodes of sleep, intoxication, and emotion. If the relevant capacities are generally there when they are required, this is coupling enough."

mcq.q: What role does the paper give language in extended cognition?
o: Language serves communication only and is unrelated to an individual's cognition
Language is a central means of extending cognition into the world
Language reduces cognitive ability because it makes us depend on symbols
Language is only a mirror of inner states and does not affect cognition
mcq.e: The paper: "language, which appears to be a central means by which cognitive processes are extended into the world... It may be that language evolved, in part, to enable such extensions of our cognitive resources within actively coupled systems."

mcq.q: What does Inga do to get to the museum?
o: She asks a friend for the address and follows the friend's directions
She hears of the exhibition, recalls from biological memory that the museum is on 53rd Street, and goes there
She uses an electronic map to find the museum since she cannot remember the address
She checks her notebook for the museum's address and then goes there
mcq.e: The paper: "Inga hears from a friend that there is an exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art, and decides to go see it. She thinks for a moment and recalls that the museum is on 53rd Street, so she walks to 53rd Street".

mcq.q: How does Otto differ from Inga?
o: Otto has Alzheimer's and uses an always-carried notebook for the function biological memory usually serves
Otto has a better memory than Inga so needs no tool to remember information
Otto has no need to go to the museum while Inga wants to see the exhibition
Otto lives in another city so does not know the museum's address as Inga does
mcq.e: The paper: "Otto suffers from Alzheimer's disease, and like many Alzheimer's patients, he relies on information in the environment to help structure his life. Otto carries a notebook around with him everywhere he goes... For Otto, his notebook plays the role usually played by a biological memory."

mcq.q: What do the authors conclude about Otto's belief?
o: Otto believes it only while reading the notebook and loses the belief when it is closed
Otto only believes the notebook says 53rd Street and has no belief about the museum's location
Otto has no belief because beliefs can exist only inside the head
Otto believed the museum was on 53rd Street even before consulting his notebook
mcq.e: The paper: "it seems reasonable to say that Otto believed the museum was on 53rd Street even before consulting his notebook. For in relevant respects the cases are entirely analogous: the notebook plays for Otto the same role that memory plays for Inga."

mcq.q: Why do the authors call explaining Otto's action via "beliefs about the notebook" needlessly complex?
o: Every explanation of action must be complex to be convincing in philosophy
The notebook is a constant for Otto as memory is for Inga
The notebook plays no role in Otto's actions so it need not appear in explanations
Otto never uses the notebook to guide his actions but only for entertainment
mcq.e: The paper: "The notebook is a constant for Otto, in the same way that memory is a constant for Inga; to point to it in every belief/desire explanation would be redundant. In an explanation, simplicity is power."

mcq.q: Who is Twin Otto and what does he illustrate?
o: Otto's friend who always goes with him to the museum and reminds him of the address
A copy of Otto on Twin Earth who knows the museum's exact address correctly
A duplicate of Otto from the skin in whose notebook mistakenly says 51st Street
Otto's twin living in another city who also has Alzheimer's like Otto
mcq.e: The paper: "Twin Otto, who is just like Otto except that a while ago he mistakenly wrote in his notebook that the Museum of Modern Art was on 51st Street... Twin Otto is best characterized as believing that the museum is on 51st Street, where Otto believes it is on 53rd."

mcq.q: How does Twin Otto differ from Putnam and Burge's cases?
o: The external feature (notebook) is active with direct impact on behavior: Otto walks to 53rd Street
Twin Otto concerns not the content of belief but only the geographic location of the pair
Twin Otto is identical to Putnam and Burge's cases in every respect the paper considers
In Putnam and Burge's cases behavior differs while in Twin Otto's it is the same
mcq.e: The paper: "In the cases we are describing, the relevant external features play an active role in the here-and-now, and have a direct impact on behaviour. Where Otto walks to 53rd Street, Twin Otto walks to 51st."

mcq.q: Which four features make notebook information count as belief?
o: Fastest, prettiest, easiest to carry and shareable with the most people
Constant, directly available, automatically endorsed on retrieval
Most expensive, rarest, hardest to access and least known to others
Newest, most accurate, shortest and confirmed by many other people
mcq.e: The paper: "First, the notebook is a constant in Otto's life... Second, the information in the notebook is directly available without difficulty. Third, upon retrieving information from the notebook he automatically endorses it. Fourth, the information in the notebook has been consciously endorsed at some point in the past".

mcq.q: What do the authors say about the fourth criterion (past conscious endorsement)?
o: It is the only criterion all three scholars agree on with no dispute
The authors do not mention this criterion in discussing conditions of belief
Its status is arguable, while the first three certainly play a crucial role
It is the most important criterion and required in every case of extended belief
mcq.e: The paper: "The status of the fourth feature as a criterion for belief is arguable (perhaps one can acquire beliefs through subliminal perception, or through memory tampering?), but the first three features certainly play a crucial role."

mcq.q: What do the authors say about the Internet becoming part of belief?
o: The Internet is likely to fail on multiple counts unless the user is unusually computer-reliant, facile and trusting
The Internet always qualifies as part of everyone's belief in all cases
The Internet can never be part of belief however dependent the user is
The authors do not mention the Internet anywhere in the paper on extended cognition
mcq.e: The paper: "The Internet is likely to fail on multiple counts, unless I am unusually computer-reliant, facile with the technology, and trusting, but information in certain files on my computer may qualify."

mcq.q: If I often act without consulting my Filofax (sometimes answering "I don't know"), what is the status of its information?
o: It is still fully part of my belief since it is in my own personal notebook
It is not belief at all since belief can exist only inside each person's head
It is stronger than biological belief since it is carefully recorded on paper
It counts less clearly as part of my beliefs
mcq.e: The paper: "if I often act without consultation—for example, if I sometimes answer relevant questions with 'I don't know'—then information in it counts less clearly as part of my belief system."

mcq.q: How does the paper treat socially extended cognition?
o: Socially extended cognition applies only to very large groups such as nations or religions
My mental states may be partly constituted by others' states, especially given high trust, reliance
Socially extended cognition occurs between any pair of people whatever their relationship
Cognition can occur only inside one individual and cannot involve others
mcq.e: The paper: "Could my mental states be partly constituted by the states of other thinkers? We see no reason why not, in principle... What is central is a high degree of trust, reliance, and accessibility."

mcq.q: What does the paper say about the self after accepting the extended mind?
o: The self shrinks to only the currently occurrent conscious states
The self is also extended: Otto is best regarded as a coupling of biological organism and external resources
The self is destroyed completely when people depend on outside tools
The self is unrelated to mind, so the paper's thesis does not affect it
mcq.e: The paper: "Does the extended mind imply an extended self? It seems so... Otto himself is best regarded as an extended system, a coupling of biological organism and external resources."

mcq.q: What moral consequence does the paper suggest?
o: There is no moral consequence since the extended mind is a purely theoretical matter
Interfering with someone's environment may have the same moral significance as interfering with their person
People have absolute rights over their environment since it is not part of the mind
Only direct interference with a person's body has any significant moral weight
mcq.e: The paper: "It may be, for example, that in some cases interfering with someone's environment will have the same moral significance as interfering with their person."

mcq.q: Why should the three papers not be treated as empirical evidence about tools in learning?
o: Because all three used very large samples but with unstandardized measures
Because all three studied only animals and not humans
Licklider and Engelbart write visions and conceptual frameworks and Clark
Because all three have since been completely refuted by later experiments
mcq.e: The three are a vision paper (1960), a conceptual-framework report (1962) and a philosophical argument (1998); the only numbers are Licklider's self-measurement, the cited Tetris timings and a small brick-pencil demonstration.

mcq.q: What separates "augmentation" from "replacement" per Licklider and Engelbart?
o: Augmentation and replacement are two names for the same automation process
Augmentation applies only to calculation and replacement to reasoning
Augmentation means the machine does everything and people only watch; replacement means people do everything
Augmentation keeps humans in charge of goals, criteria and evaluation and raises the capability of the whole system
mcq.e: Licklider: people set goals, criteria and evaluation, machines do routine work; not "mechanically extended man" or automation. Engelbart: not raising native intelligence but augmenting the H-LAM/T system.

mcq.q: Why does Engelbart treat "Training" and "Methodology" as components of the augmentation system?
o: Because Engelbart cared only about hardware and ignored the human factor throughout the report
Because training and methodology are minor extras that do not affect the system's effectiveness
Because automatic tools suffice to augment intellect without people learning or having methods
Because tools are effective only when people are trained and have methods to organize their use
mcq.e: Engelbart: the system to improve is "a trained human being together with his artifacts, language, and methodology"; tools are one of four means.

mcq.q: In the thesis, by Licklider, which part should students keep when using AI (design inference)?
o: No part, since AI will do everything from goal setting to evaluating results
All of the coding, with AI allowed only to check spelling in the student's report
Only data entry, since all reasoning should be done by AI entirely
Planning, predicting, setting criteria and evaluating results
mcq.e: Design inference from Licklider's division of labor: people set goals, criteria and evaluation; machines do routine work. What is worth measuring is which part the AI is carrying.

mcq.q: What does the "free AI use" group lack in the H-LAM/T system compared with a treatment group taught methods (design inference)?
o: The tool (A), since the control group is not allowed any tools
The human (H), since the control group has no students taking part
Methodology and training (M and T), though it has the tool (A)
Language (L), since the control group has no language to talk to the AI
mcq.e: Design inference linking Engelbart: the treatment group is taught a method (Socratic, self-explanation) and trained; the control group has tools but lacks M and T.

mcq.q: If AI is part of a coupled cognitive system, what does a test with AI removed measure (design inference)?
o: The capability of the student-plus-AI system, since AI remains part of the system when removed
Nothing, since removing AI erases all of the student's capability entirely
The capability of the biological part standing alone
The capability of the AI, since the student contributes nothing once AI is taken away
mcq.e: Clark and Chalmers: removing an external component lowers system competence "as if removing part of its brain"; so a no-AI test measures the biological part alone; a design inference to state when interpreting RQ1.

mcq.q: How could Otto's first three criteria serve as indicators of AI dependence (design inference)?
o: Ask: does the student almost always ask AI, find it readily accessible
Ask: does the student believe AI is smarter than his or her instructor in every field?
Ask: does the student remember exactly the answers to every question once asked of AI?
Ask: does the student own a paper notebook that is carried everywhere at all times?
mcq.e: Design inference: the three criteria (constant, available, automatically endorsed) describe the degree of coupling; applied to AI they indicate dependence (link to Module 10).

mcq.q: Does "the extended mind" say whether dependence on tools is good or bad for learning?
o: No; it only sets conditions for counting a tool as part of cognition
Yes; it states dependence on tools is always bad for learning and should be limited
Yes; it states dependence on tools is always good for learning and should be encouraged
Yes; it gives empirical evidence of tools' effects on students' scores
mcq.e: Clark and Chalmers discuss the boundary of mind and belief, not learning outcomes; the link to the thesis is design inference.

essay.q: Present Licklider's (1960) concept of man-computer symbiosis: distinguish it from "mechanically extended man" and automation, state the two main aims and the anticipated division of labor between human and machine.
essay.m: Hint: Symbiosis: intimate living together of two dissimilar organisms (fig tree and Blastophaga); no man-computer symbiosis existed in 1960. Distinctions: mechanically extended man (human supplies initiative, direction, criterion; machine only extends) and semi-automatic systems (humanly extended machines). Two aims: bring machines into the formulative part of problems and into real-time thinking. Division: people set goals, hypotheses, questions, criteria, evaluate, handle low-probability cases; machines do routine work, simulation, data transformation.

essay.q: Analyze Licklider's evidence about "thinking time" (85%) and give three limits of using it to support his claims.
essay.m: Hint: Self-tracking in spring and summer 1957, one person as own subject; 85% of time getting into position to think, decide, learn; the six speech-intelligibility measurements example. Limits: one-person sample and not representative (the author admits); self-classified activities; an example from 1957, not evidence for all fields; says nothing about generative AI.

essay.q: Explain Engelbart's H-LAM/T system: the four means, the capability hierarchy, and why "intelligence amplification" does not mean raising native intelligence. Apply it to a programming class with AI.
essay.m: Hint: Artifacts, Language, Methodology, Training; an interknit capability hierarchy (writing prose is a subprocess of higher processes); a change at one level affects others; synergistic structuring; the augmented entity is the whole system. Application (design inference): a programming class with AI has tools (A), a programming language and terminology (L), methods (M: Socratic, self-explanation) and training (T); the control group lacks M and T.

essay.q: Present the parity principle and the Inga and Otto example of Clark and Chalmers (1998) and the four criteria for outside information to count as belief. Evaluate whether a student's use of AI meets those criteria.
essay.m: Hint: Parity: a part of the world playing a role that, in the head, we would call cognitive is part of cognition. Inga (biological memory) and Otto (notebook); Twin Otto. Four criteria: constant, available, automatically endorsed, previously endorsed. Evaluation (design inference): a student who always asks AI, finds it easy to reach, and automatically accepts its (unverified) output may meet the first three criteria; but the paper does not say whether this is good or bad for learning; the Internet in general fails many criteria unless the user is very reliant.

essay.q: Compare the three papers (Licklider, Engelbart, Clark and Chalmers) on question, unit of analysis, role of the human and kind of evidence, then choose the strongest point to defend your treatment design.
essay.m: Hint: Licklider: division of labor (humans keep goals, criteria, evaluation); Engelbart: the H-LAM/T system (role of training and methods); Clark and Chalmers: the boundary of mind and coupling conditions. Evidence: all are visions or arguments. Defense: the treatment teaches method and training (Engelbart) and keeps goals and evaluation with students (Licklider); use Otto's three criteria as dependence indicators. Limit: none of the three papers has empirical evidence on generative AI.

essay.q: If AI is treated as part of a coupled cognitive system, argue why the thesis should still measure ability with AI removed for RQ1, and state what must be explained when reporting results.
essay.m: Hint: Clark and Chalmers: removing an external component lowers system capability "as if removing part of the brain"; so there are two questions (the student-plus-AI system, the biological part alone). The educational goal is independent ability (transfer, working without AI). State that RQ1 measures the biological part alone, and add a with-AI measure for completeness; avoid concluding "dependence is bad" merely because no-AI scores are lower.
